question: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left), Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Tilly Metz (Verts/ALE), Sigrid Friis (Renew), Villy Søvndal (Verts/ALE), Manuela Ripa (PPE), Tomáš Kubín (PfE), Rasmus Nordqvist (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Whale strandings in European waters are not isolated incidents, but can signal broader ecosystem disturbances. The recent case of ‘Timmy’ in the Baltic Sea highlights cumulative pressures such as underwater noise, bycatch, ghost nets and pollution, and underlines the need for coordinated action at EU level. Under frameworks such as the EU Habitats Directive and the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, stranded whales are protected species and important indicators of marine ecosystem health. Their deaths may point to shortcomings in mitigating human-induced pressures and gaps in monitoring, coordination and prevention. While instruments such as Council Regulation (EC) No 812/2004, the Agreement on the Conservation of Small Cetaceans of the Baltic, North East Atlantic, Irish and North Seas and the Agreement on the Conservation of Cetaceans of the Black Sea, Mediterranean Sea and contiguous Atlantic Area address bycatch, monitoring and regional cooperation, they do not provide for a comprehensive, EU-wide emergency response mechanism for strandings. By contrast, several non-EU countries have established coordinated national response systems. In the light of the increasing number of strandings and the fragmented policy landscape: 1.
What actions is the Commission taking to protect marine ecosystems, in particular cetaceans?
Does the Commission intend to propose a coordinated EU-wide emergency plan for whale and marine mammal strandings?
How does the Commission assess the effectiveness of current EU and regional frameworks in responding to and preventing whale strandings?

(7 July 2026) The long-term protection and recovery of cetaceans and marine ecosystems on which they depend is ensured through a comprehensive EU legal framework. The Habitats Directive (1) requires Member States to establish a system of strict protection for certain specie s (2) prohibiting their deliberate disturbance, capture or killing, and safeguarding their breeding and resting areas, complemented where appropriate by the designation of Natura 2000 sites. The directive also requires Member States to establish a system to monitor incidental capture and killing of cetaceans and take appropriate preventive measures. The Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) (3) requires Member States to achieve good environmental status of their marine waters, including by reducing pressures like bycatch, underwater noise and pollution.

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7-50. Including all cetaceans. Directive 2008/56/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 June 2008 establishing a framework for community action in the field of marine environmental policy, OJ L 164, 25.6.2008, pp. 19-40.

The common fisheries policy (4) aims to minimise and, where possible, eliminate incidental catches of sensitive species (5). The Commission also works with regional fisheries management organisations to protect vulnerable species from interactions with fisheries (6), promotes consistent maritime spatial planning to minimise conflicts at sea, and supports Member States with guidance documents (7), funding opportunities (8), and by taking legal action where appropriate (9). The Commission considers that, due to the specific nature of individual cases, whale and marine mammal strandings are most appropriately dealt with by national and regional authorities. Member States have sufficient tools under the existing legal framework to take such action. The Commission assesses (10) Member States’ marine strategies under the MSFD and provides guidance (11). It is currently working on reviewing (12) the directive, following its recent evaluation (13).

For this endeavour, the Commission supports Member States in adopting bycatch mitigation measures through regionalisation, such as those adopted for harbour porpoises in the Baltic Sea and common dolphins in the Bay of Biscay. This is for example, the case in the Mediterranean and Black Sea where the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) adopted in 2023 a regional plan of action to monitor and mitigate interactions between fisheries and vulnerable species. The latter includes a call to promote the harmonised and standardised collection of stranding data.
